## Ecological Background

American mastodons (*Mammut americanum*) were large Pleistocene forest-dwelling browsers (~8,000 kg body mass) inhabiting North America and Eurasia until ~10–11 ka BP, with *Picea* spp. forming a major component of their diet (Birks et al., 2018; Teale & Miller, 2012; Larramendi, 2015).

Here mastodons occupy the landscape at an initial density of 1.5 individuals per 100 ha (120 kg ha⁻¹; Bakker et al., 2016) with 1% yr⁻¹ logistic population growth. Alongside browsing trees up to ~4 m height (Guy, 1976), they uproot small-diameter Norway spruce (*Picea abies*) stems similarly to modern African elephants (Shannon et al., 2008; Scheiter & Higgins, 2012).

## Model Implementation

Like roe deer, mastodons use `BiteDistribution` across 1000 m cells without a spatial dispersal kernel. Carrying capacity in `BiteBiomass` combines foliage biomass from all Norway spruce saplings and trees with dbh ≤ 15 cm.

`BiteImpact` demonstrates pairing sapling browsing (`target: 'browsing'`) with uprooting mortality (`target: 'tree'`). The second code tab provides three alternative `BiteImpact` configurations showing how to stratify uprooting probabilities by DBH or tree height class.
